title: FV, PV and the sign convention
summary: Excel solves time-value problems with five numbers: rate, periods, payment, present value and future value. FV moves money forward, PV brings it back, and the signs say which way the money flows.
objectives: Name the five time-value arguments: rate, nper, pmt, pv and fv.
Use FV to grow a lump sum and PV to discount a future amount.
Apply Excel’s sign convention: money out is negative, money in is positive.
Match the rate to the period when compounding monthly.

slides.h: Five numbers describe every TVM problem
p: Every time-value problem has the same five parts. Excel’s finance functions take them as arguments; give four and a function finds the fifth.
**FV** finds fv, **PV** finds pv, **PMT** finds pmt, **NPER** finds nper and **RATE** finds rate.
Lesson 1.3 adds pmt: savings every month.
Learn the five names once; they come back in every lesson of this course.
In real life: writes the five numbers on a sticky note before she opens Excel: rate, periods, payment, now, later. One of them is the “?”, and that tells her which function to use.

slides.h: The sign convention: money out is negative
p: Excel looks at money from **your** side. Money you hand over is negative; money you get back is positive. Put the deposit in as −1,00,000 and FV comes back positive.
Deposit, investment, loan repayment: **negative** (it leaves your pocket).
Maturity amount, loan received, pension: **positive** (it comes in).
Got a negative answer you didn’t expect? Flip the sign of an input, or put a minus in front of the function.
In real life: gets a negative EMI on day one and thinks Excel is broken. Their manager’s rule: “Excel isn’t wrong; it’s telling you which way the money goes.”

slides.h: FV: what a lump sum grows to
p: `=FV(rate, nper, pmt, pv)` grows a present value forward. With no regular payment, put 0 for pmt.
FV gives exactly the compound-interest answer from Lesson 1.1.
The minus in **-B2** turns the deposit into money paid out.
FV saves you writing the power formula, and it handles regular payments too.
In real life: keeps one sheet with every deposit she holds, each with an FV formula. She knows what each will pay out without waiting for the bank’s letter.

check.q: Meera deposits ₹2,00,000 for 3 years at 6%. Which formula shows the maturity amount as a positive number?
check.explain: The deposit leaves her pocket, so it goes in as −2,00,000, and FV comes back positive.

why.0: That treats the deposit as money received, so FV comes back negative.
why.2: That puts ₹2 lakh in as a payment every year.
why.3: PV goes backwards in time, not forwards.

p: To reach a future amount, how much must you put in **today**? Discount the future amount back with PV.
₹20 lakh in 10 years at 8% is worth ₹9,26,387 today.
PV is negative here: it’s money you put in to get ₹20 lakh back.
**Discounting** is compounding in reverse: divide by (1 + r)^n instead of multiplying.
In real life: wants ₹20 lakh for her son’s college in 10 years. At 8% a year she needs ₹9,26,387 invested today, not ₹20 lakh.

visual.resultNote: negative: you must pay this in today

p: ₹10 lakh today or ₹13 lakh in four years? Bring the later amount back to today and compare like with like.
At 8%, ₹13 lakh in 4 years is worth ₹9,55,539 today: take the ₹10 lakh now.
At 6%, it’s worth ₹10,29,722 today: wait for the ₹13 lakh.
The discount rate decides. Use the return you could really earn on the money.
In real life: was offered ₹10 lakh now or ₹13 lakh in four years for a strip of land the highway needed. His son worked out both at the bank’s deposit rate before they signed.

slides.h: Match the rate to the period
p: If interest compounds monthly, use a **monthly** rate and count **months**: divide the yearly rate by 12 and multiply the years by 12.
rate and nper must use the **same** period: months with months, years with years.
Monthly: rate/12 and years*12. Quarterly: rate/4 and years*4.
Mixing them (a yearly rate with 36 periods) is the commonest finance mistake in Excel.
In real life: found a colleague’s EMI calculator treating 9% as a monthly rate: the yearly rate had gone in with months as the periods. Its EMIs were several times too high.

check.q: Which gives today’s value of ₹5,00,000 due in 6 years, at 7% a year, as a positive number?
check.explain: PV returns a negative number (money you’d put in); the minus in front flips it to positive. =PV(7%,6,0,-500000) works too.

why.2: That grows the money forward instead of bringing it back.
why.3: A monthly rate with 6 periods mixes months and years.

demo.intro: Use Excel’s FV and PV functions on Meera’s deposit and her sister’s college goal.

frames.say: In **B6**, `=FV(B3,B4,0,-B2)`. The minus makes the deposit money paid out, so the answer, ₹1,40,255, is positive.
For the goal, **Formulas › Financial › PV**. Rate **B10**, Nper **B11**, Pmt **0**, Fv **-B9**: put in ₹9,26,387 today.

callouts.text: Minus B9, so the answer shows positive

frames.say: The finished PV formula in **B12**. With Fv as −B9 the answer is positive; with +B9 it would show −9,26,387.
For monthly compounding, divide the rate and multiply the years by 12: `=FV(E10/12,E11*12,0,-E9)`.

tasks.prompt: In **B6**, use **FV** to work out what Meera’s ₹1,00,000 deposit is worth at the end.
hints: FV(rate, nper, pmt, pv): there’s no regular payment, so pmt is 0.
The deposit is money paid out, so pass it as -B2.

mistakes.msg: That makes B2 a payment every year. A single deposit goes in pv, the fourth argument: FV(B3,B4,0,-B2).

tasks.prompt: In **B12**, use **PV** to work out how much must be invested **today** to have B9 in B11 years, as a positive amount.
hints: PV(rate, nper, pmt, fv): pmt is 0 and fv is the amount needed.
Pass the future amount as -B9 so the answer comes back positive.

mistakes.msg: That’s FV, which moves money forward. To find today’s amount, use PV.

hints: Look at the sign of the pv argument.

tasks.explain: Positive pv means Meera received ₹1 lakh, so at the end she would owe ₹1,40,255: negative. Pass -B2, or put a minus in front of FV.

quiz.q: Which argument is the number of periods?
quiz.explain: nper: how many periods the money stays invested or borrowed.

quiz.q: In Excel’s sign convention, a deposit you make is…
quiz.explain: Money that leaves your pocket is negative.
1,000 paid in grows to 1,210, received back: positive.
You’d pay in 1,000 today to receive 1,210 in two years, so PV is −1,000.

quiz.q: Monthly compounding at 12% a year for 5 years. Which rate and nper?
₹8 lakh today, or ₹10 lakh in 3 years. You can earn 9% a year. Which is worth more?
quiz.explain: ₹10 lakh in 3 years at 9% is worth only ₹7,72,183 today, less than ₹8 lakh in hand.

why.0: More rupees, but later: bring it back to today with PV before comparing.
why.3: PV brings both to the same date.

points: Five arguments: **rate, nper, pmt, pv, fv** (and **type**). Give four, and a function finds the fifth.
**Sign convention**: money paid out is negative, money received is positive. Pass `-B2`, or put a minus before the function.
**FV** moves money forward, **PV** brings it back; with monthly compounding use **rate/12** and **years×12**.
